question: Y130
answer:
# DRAFT — WITHDRAWAL PERIOD UNDER DIRECTIVE 2011/83/EU: SERVICE CONTRACTS AND SALES CONTRACTS

**To:** Supervising attorney / [Retailer] compliance
**From:** Drafting attorney
**Re:** When the withdrawal period expires for (a) a service contract and (b) a sales contract; draft withdrawal instructions for an online retailer
**Jurisdiction:** European Union. Directive 2011/83/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 25 October 2011 on consumer rights, amending Council Directive 93/13/EEC and Directive 1999/44/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council and repealing Council Directive 85/577/EEC and Directive 97/7/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council (Text with EEA relevance), OJ L 304, 22.11.2011, p. 64 (CELEX 32011L0083) — cited below as "the Directive". The Directive binds as to result and is given effect through the national transposing measure of the Member State of sale; no Member State has been specified, so the rule stated here is the Directive-level rule and §7 lists what must be verified against the transposing law before the instructions go live.
**Status:** Draft for review by a qualified attorney. Not legal advice.

---

## 1. ANSWER

### 1.1 Service contract — 14 days from the day of conclusion

> "2. Without prejudice to Article 10, the withdrawal period referred to in paragraph 1 of this Article shall expire after 14 days from: (a) in the case of service contracts, the day of the conclusion of the contract;"
> — Directive, Art 9(2)(a).

**Rule:** the period expires **14 days after the day of the conclusion of the contract**. The day of conclusion is the trigger and is not counted as day 1. The date on which performance begins, the invoice date and the payment date are irrelevant.

**Worked example:** contract concluded Tuesday 3 March 2026 → the period expires at the end of **Tuesday 17 March 2026**. A withdrawal communication sent on 17 March is in time (Art 11(1); Annex I(A): "To meet the withdrawal deadline, it is sufficient for you to send your communication concerning your exercise of the right of withdrawal before the withdrawal period has expired.").

### 1.2 Sales contract — 14 days from the day physical possession is acquired

> "(b) in the case of sales contracts, the day on which the consumer or a third party other than the carrier and indicated by the consumer acquires physical possession of the goods or: (i) in the case of multiple goods ordered by the consumer in one order and delivered separately, the day on which the consumer or a third party other than the carrier and indicated by the consumer acquires physical possession of the last good; (ii) in the case of delivery of a good consisting of multiple lots or pieces, the day on which the consumer or a third party other than the carrier and indicated by the consumer acquires physical possession of the last lot or piece; (iii) in the case of contracts for regular delivery of goods during defined period of time, the day on which the consumer or a third party other than the carrier and indicated by the consumer acquires physical possession of the first good;"
> — Directive, Art 9(2)(b).

**Rule:** the period expires **14 days after the day the consumer, or a third party other than the carrier indicated by the consumer, acquires physical possession of the goods**. The trigger is *possession*, not dispatch, not the carrier's first delivery attempt, and not the conclusion of the contract. The four sub-cases:

| Case | Trigger day | Directive provision |
|---|---|---|
| Single good | Possession of the goods | Art 9(2)(b) |
| Multiple goods, one order, delivered separately | Possession of the **last** good | Art 9(2)(b)(i) |
| One good delivered in multiple lots or pieces | Possession of the **last** lot or piece | Art 9(2)(b)(ii) |
| Regular delivery of goods during a defined period (e.g. subscription box) | Possession of the **first** good | Art 9(2)(b)(iii) |

**Worked examples (2026):**
- Single good received Friday 20 March 2026 → expires **Friday 3 April 2026**.
- Two goods ordered together, delivered 20 March and 27 March 2026 → trigger is 27 March; expires **Friday 10 April 2026**.
- Subscription with first delivery 3 March 2026 and monthly deliveries thereafter → trigger is 3 March; expires **Tuesday 17 March 2026**, notwithstanding that deliveries continue.

The consumer may exercise the right before acquiring possession: recital 40 of the Directive states that "the consumer should be able to exercise the right to withdraw before acquiring physical possession of the goods", and Art 11(1) requires only that the consumer inform the trader "[b]efore the expiry of the withdrawal period".

### 1.3 Both limbs are subject to the Article 10 overlay

Article 9(2) opens with the words "Without prejudice to Article 10". The complete answer therefore has three layers:

> "Article 10 — Omission of information on the right of withdrawal. 1. If the trader has not provided the consumer with the information on the right of withdrawal as required by point (h) of Article 6(1), the withdrawal period shall expire 12 months from the end of the initial withdrawal period, as determined in accordance with Article 9(2). 2. If the trader has provided the consumer with the information provided for in paragraph 1 of this Article within 12 months from the day referred to in Article 9(2), the withdrawal period shall expire 14 days after the day upon which the consumer receives that information."
> — Directive, Art 10.

- **Layer 1 (compliance):** 14 days as set out in §1.1 / §1.2.
- **Layer 2 (no Art 6(1)(h) information):** 12 months from the end of the initial 14-day period. Service contract concluded 3 March 2026, no withdrawal information given → initial period ends 17 March 2026; the period expires **17 March 2027**.
- **Layer 3 (late cure):** if the information is supplied within that 12-month window, the period expires 14 days after the day the consumer receives it. Information received 1 June 2026 → expires **15 June 2026**.

The Article 6(1)(h) information is: "where a right of withdrawal is not provided for in accordance with Article 16, the information that the consumer will not benefit from a right of withdrawal or, where applicable, the circumstances under which the consumer loses his right of withdrawal" and, where the right exists, "the conditions, time limit and procedures for exercising that right in accordance with Article 9(1) and (2), as well as the model withdrawal form set out in Annex I(B)". The commercial consequence is that a defective information notice converts a 14-day exposure into a 12-month exposure on every order — this, not the 14-day computation, is where the drafting risk sits.

### 1.4 Where no period runs at all

> "Article 16 — Exceptions from the right of withdrawal. Member States shall not provide for the right of withdrawal set out in Articles 9 to 15 in respect of distance and off-premises contracts as regards the following: …"
> — Directive, Art 16.

Material to a service retailer: **Art 16(a)** — a service contract "after the service has been fully performed" where "the performance began with the consumer's prior express consent and acknowledgement that he loses his right of withdrawal". Where Art 16(a) is satisfied the period does not so much expire as become moot; where it is not satisfied (no express consent, or performance incomplete) the Art 9 period runs and the consumer who withdraws owes a proportionate payment under Art 14. Note for file: the project analysis referred to "Article 16(l)" for loss of the right on full performance; that is wrong — Art 16(l) concerns digital content not supplied on a tangible medium. Full performance of a service is Art 16(a).

### 1.5 Adjacent case: digital content and mixed contracts

- Digital content not supplied on a tangible medium (and water, gas, electricity not sold in a limited volume or set quantity, and district heating): the trigger is "the day of the conclusion of the contract" — Directive, Art 9(2)(c).
- A contract having as its object both goods and services is a **sales contract**: "'sales contract' means any contract under which the trader transfers or undertakes to transfer the ownership of goods to the consumer and the consumer pays or undertakes to pay the price thereof, including any contract having as its object both goods and services" — Directive, Art 2(6). So a bundled goods-plus-installation or goods-plus-service order takes the **possession** trigger in Art 9(2)(b), not the conclusion trigger in Art 9(2)(a).
- "'service contract' means any contract other than a sales contract under which the trader supplies or undertakes to supply a service to the consumer and the consumer pays or undertakes to pay the price thereof" — Directive, Art 2(1). Classification is therefore exhaustive and mutually exclusive: everything that is not a sales contract and not within Art 9(2)(c) falls under Art 9(2)(a).

---

## 2. COMPUTATION METHOD (for the retailer's systems)

1. **Identify the contract type** using Art 2(1), 2(6) and Art 9(2)(c). Mixed goods/services = sales contract.
2. **Capture the correct trigger date** in the order record:
   - services / digital content without tangible medium: the contract-conclusion timestamp (order confirmation), not the service start date;
   - goods: the **proof-of-delivery / possession** date from the carrier, not the dispatch date; for split shipments capture the date of the **last** delivery line; for multi-lot consignments the **last** lot; for regular-delivery subscriptions the **first** delivery.
3. **Add 14 calendar days** to the trigger date; do not count the trigger day. The resulting date is the last day on which a withdrawal communication is in time.
4. **Check the information notice actually delivered with that order.** If the Art 6(1)(h) information was not given, apply Art 10(1): expiry is 12 months from the end of the date computed in step 3; if it was given late, apply Art 10(2): expiry is 14 days after the day the consumer received it.
5. **Do not roll the date forward** for weekends or public holidays on the face of the Directive — the Directive is silent and the point is governed by national law (§7.2).
6. **Store the trigger date and the computed expiry date** on the order record; the burden of showing that the information was given and when possession was acquired is the trader's.

---

## 3. CONSEQUENCES OF WITHDRAWAL (needed because the instructions must state them)

- **Reimbursement:** the trader reimburses all payments received, including the costs of delivery (except supplementary costs for a delivery type other than the least expensive standard delivery offered), without undue delay and in any event not later than 14 days from the day it is informed, by the same means of payment and with no fee to the consumer — Directive, Art 14.
- **Return costs:** borne by the consumer where the trader has informed the consumer of that obligation, unless the trader agreed to bear them; the model instructions require the trader to select the applicable statement — Directive, Annex I(A) ("Effects of withdrawal").
- **Diminished value:** the consumer is liable only for diminished value resulting from handling beyond what is necessary to establish the nature, characteristics and functioning of the goods — Directive, Annex I(A) ("Effects of withdrawal"), to be stated in the instructions.
- **Proportionate payment for services begun early:** "If you requested to begin the performance of services … during the withdrawal period, you shall pay us an amount which is in proportion to what has been provided until you have communicated us your withdrawal from this contract, in comparison with the full coverage of the contract." — Directive, Annex I(A).
- **Performance during the period is permitted:** "The Member States shall not prohibit the contracting parties from performing their contractual obligations during the withdrawal period" — Directive, Art 9(3); in the case of off-premises contracts Member States may maintain existing national rules prohibiting collection of payment in that window (Art 9(3), second sentence).

---

## 4. DRAFT — WITHDRAWAL INSTRUCTIONS (SCHEDULE TO BE PUBLISHED AT CHECKOUT AND SENT ON A DURABLE MEDIUM)

*Drafting note: the wording below follows the model instructions in Annex I(A) of the Directive. Annex I(A) prescribes the model text; the trader selects the applicable variant and fills the bracketed fields. Counsel must check the wording letter-for-letter against Annex I(A) and Annex I(B) in the CELEX text before publication (§7.1).*

### 4.1 Right of withdrawal

> **Right of withdrawal**
>
> You have the right to withdraw from this contract within 14 days without giving any reason.
>
> The withdrawal period will expire after 14 days from the day **[select one]**
> - *(services / digital content not on a tangible medium)* of the conclusion of the contract.
> - *(sales — single good)* on which you acquire, or a third party other than the carrier and indicated by you acquires, physical possession of the goods.
> - *(sales — multiple goods ordered in one order and delivered separately)* on which you acquire, or a third party other than the carrier and indicated by you acquires, physical possession of the last good.
> - *(sales — good consisting of multiple lots or pieces)* on which you acquire, or a third party other than the carrier and indicated by you acquires, physical possession of the last lot or piece.
> - *(sales — regular delivery of goods during a defined period of time)* on which you acquire, or a third party other than the carrier and indicated by you acquires, physical possession of the first good.
>
> To exercise the right of withdrawal, you must inform us **[trader name, geographical address, telephone number, fax number and e-mail address]** of your decision to withdraw from this contract by an unequivocal statement (e.g. a letter sent by post, fax or e-mail). You may use the attached model withdrawal form, but it is not obligatory.
>
> **[If the website route is offered]** You can also fill in and submit the model withdrawal form or any other unequivocal statement on our website **[internet address]**. If you use this option, we will communicate to you an acknowledgement of receipt of such a withdrawal on a durable medium (e.g. by e-mail) without delay.
>
> To meet the withdrawal deadline, it is sufficient for you to send your communication concerning your exercise of the right of withdrawal before the withdrawal period has expired.

### 4.2 Effects of withdrawal

> **Effects of withdrawal**
>
> If you withdraw from this contract, we shall reimburse to you all payments received from you, including the costs of delivery (with the exception of the supplementary costs resulting from your choice of a type of delivery other than the least expensive type of standard delivery offered by us), without undue delay and in any event not later than 14 days from the day on which we are informed about your decision to withdraw from this contract. We will carry out such reimbursement using the same means of payment as you used for the initial transaction, unless you have expressly agreed otherwise; in any event, you will not incur any fees as a result of such reimbursement.
>
> **[Sales contracts]** We may withhold reimbursement until we have received the goods back or you have supplied evidence of having sent back the goods, whichever is the earliest.
>
> **[Select one — return costs]**
> - We will collect the goods at our own expense.
> - You will have to bear the direct cost of returning the goods.
> - You will have to bear the direct cost of returning the goods if their value exceeds EUR **[amount]**.
>
> You are only liable for any diminished value of the goods resulting from the handling other than what is necessary to establish the nature, characteristics and functioning of the goods.
>
> **[Services / utilities begun early]** If you requested to begin the performance of services during the withdrawal period, you shall pay us an amount which is in proportion to what has been provided until you have communicated us your withdrawal from this contract, in comparison with the full coverage of the contract.

### 4.3 Model withdrawal form (Annex I(B)) — to be attached

> **Model withdrawal form**
> *(complete and return this form only if you wish to withdraw from the contract)*
> — To **[trader name, geographical address, fax number and e-mail address]**:
> — I/We (*) hereby give notice that I/We (*) withdraw from my/our (*) contract of sale of the following goods (*)/for the provision of the following service (*),
> — Ordered on (*)/received on (*),
> — Name of consumer(s),
> — Address of consumer(s),
> — Signature of consumer(s) (only if this form is notified on paper),
> — Date
> (*) Delete as appropriate.

### 4.4 Statements to be inserted where Article 16 applies

The instructions must state, where the right is excluded, "the information that the consumer will not benefit from a right of withdrawal or, where applicable, the circumstances under which the consumer loses his right of withdrawal" — Directive, Art 6(1)(h). For a service retailer that means an express statement of the Art 16(a) condition (prior express consent plus acknowledgement of loss of the right, service fully performed) and, for digital content, the Art 16(l) condition (prior express consent plus acknowledgement, performance begun).

### 4.5 Internal drafting rules

1. Never compute the expiry from the dispatch date or the order date for goods.
2. Capture the delivery/possession date from the carrier's proof of delivery and keep it for the limitation period.
3. For split shipments, key the trigger to the **last** delivery; for subscriptions, to the **first**.
4. Where the goods-plus-service bundle is a single contract, use the possession trigger (Art 2(6)).
5. Log, per order, which version of the withdrawal notice was delivered and when; that log is the defence to an Art 10 claim.
6. State the actual number of days (14) and the actual trigger event in the notice — do not paraphrase it as "within two weeks of purchase".

---

## 5. SOURCE TABLE (primary sources, cited in full)

| Point | Source |
|---|---|
| 14-day period; start dates for services, goods and utilities/digital content | Directive 2011/83/EU, OJ L 304, 22.11.2011, p. 64, Art 9(1), 9(2)(a), 9(2)(b)(i)–(iii), 9(2)(c) |
| Performance permitted during the period | Directive 2011/83/EU, Art 9(3) |
| 12-month extension and 14-day reset for omitted information | Directive 2011/83/EU, Art 10(1), 10(2) |
| Manner of exercising the right; no formal requirements beyond Annex I(B) | Directive 2011/83/EU, Art 11(1) |
| Information duty (conditions, time limit, procedures, model form) | Directive 2011/83/EU, Art 6(1)(h) |
| Definitions of service contract and sales contract (incl. mixed contracts) | Directive 2011/83/EU, Art 2(1), 2(6) |
| Exceptions (full performance of a service; digital content) | Directive 2011/83/EU, Art 16(a), 16(l) |
| Reimbursement within 14 days, same means of payment, no fees | Directive 2011/83/EU, Art 14 |
| Model instructions and model withdrawal form | Directive 2011/83/EU, Annex I(A), Annex I(B) |
| Right exercisable before possession is acquired | Directive 2011/83/EU, recital 40 |
| Amending act to be reflected in the consolidated CELEX text | Directive (EU) 2019/2161, OJ L 328, 18.12.2019, p. 7 |

---

## 6. ONE-LINE ANSWER FOR THE INSTRUCTIONS TEMPLATE

**Service contract:** 14 days from the day the contract is concluded. **Sales contract:** 14 days from the day the consumer (or a third party other than the carrier indicated by the consumer) takes physical possession — of the last good where goods ordered together are delivered separately, of the last lot or piece where the good is delivered in lots, and of the first good for regular deliveries over a defined period. In both cases, if the withdrawal information was not given, the period is 12 months from the end of that initial period, reduced to 14 days from the day the consumer receives the information if it is supplied within those 12 months.

---

## 7. VERIFICATION POINTS BEFORE PUBLICATION

**7.1 Text version.** The analysis uses the consolidated CELEX 32011L0083 text. Counsel should confirm on the face of the consolidation that Articles 9 and 10 read as quoted (no amendment to those Articles is known to this draft) and should check the Annex I(A) and Annex I(B) wording letter-for-letter, since the model text is prescribed and cannot be paraphrased.

**7.2 Member State law — not assumed, must be checked.** The Directive is a minimum-harmonisation instrument in the respects relevant here; the following are governed by the national transposing measure and no view is expressed on them:
- whether a period expiring on a Saturday, Sunday or public holiday is extended to the next working day;
- any language requirement for the withdrawal instructions;
- any national rule, permitted by Art 9(3) for off-premises contracts, restricting collection of payment during the withdrawal period;
- national rules on when a contract is "concluded" in the relevant sales channel;
- any sector-specific exclusion or extension.

**7.3 Scope assumptions.** The retailer sells to consumers (B2C) by distance contract, so Art 9 applies subject to Art 16; no Member State has been identified; no assertion is made about the law of any particular Member State.

**7.4 United Kingdom (flag only).** The UK is not an EU Member State. If the retailer sells into the UK, the assimilated version of the Directive applies through the Consumer Contracts (Information, Cancellation and Additional Charges) Regulations 2013 (SI 2013/3134), and that instrument — not the Directive — must be checked separately.

question: Y140
answer:
MEMORANDUM — APPLICABILITY OF THE FEDERAL RULES OF EVIDENCE TO FURTHER PROCEDURE IN AN ACTION PENDING ON JULY 1, 1975

Jurisdiction: United States federal courts. Draft for attorney review; not legal advice. All statements of law are tied to the primary sources cited; items I could not verify against a primary source are flagged in Part VIII and must be cite-checked before use.

=====================================================================
PART I. QUESTIONS PRESENTED
=====================================================================

1. Under the original applicability provisions of the Federal Rules of Evidence, do the Rules govern further procedure in an action that was already pending when the Rules took effect?

2. What happens to the extent that applying the Rules to that further procedure would not be feasible or would work injustice?

=====================================================================
PART II. SHORT ANSWERS
=====================================================================

1. YES. The Rules presumptively govern the further procedure in an action, case, or proceeding pending on the effective date. Section 1 of the enacting Act provides that the Rules "also apply to further procedure in actions, cases, and proceedings then pending." Pub. L. No. 93-595, § 1, 88 Stat. 1926 (Jan. 2, 1975) (reprinted as "Effective Date and Application of Rules" in the notes to the Federal Rules of Evidence, 28 U.S.C. app.).

2. TO THAT EXTENT, THE FORMER EVIDENTIARY PRINCIPLES APPLY INSTEAD. The same sentence carves out an exception: application of the Rules to pending proceedings is required "except to the extent that application of the rules would not be feasible, or would work injustice, in which event former evidentiary principles apply." Id. The exception is measured "to the extent that" — it is a partial, issue-by-issue displacement, not an all-or-nothing election between the old and new regimes.

=====================================================================
PART III. GOVERNING TEXT
=====================================================================

A. The operative provision (verified verbatim)

Pub. L. No. 93-595, § 1, 88 Stat. 1926 (Jan. 2, 1975):

"That the following rules shall take effect on the one hundred and eightieth day [July 1, 1975] beginning after the date of the enactment of this Act [Jan. 2, 1975]. These rules apply to actions, cases, and proceedings brought after the rules take effect. These rules also apply to further procedure in actions, cases, and proceedings then pending, except to the extent that application of the rules would not be feasible, or would work injustice, in which event former evidentiary principles apply."

(Quoted from the official text as reproduced in the Federal Rules of Evidence, "Effective Date and Application of Rules," Pub. L. 93-595, § 1, Jan. 2, 1975, 88 Stat. 1926, at https://www.law.cornell.edu/rules/fre.)

The bracketed July 1, 1975 date is the codifier's annotation. It is arithmetically correct: counting 180 days from January 2, 1975 yields July 1, 1975.

B. Structural point that controls the analysis

The pending-actions rule is NOT in Rule 1101. Rule 1101 (as amended) addresses (a) which courts and judges the Rules reach, (b) which classes of cases and proceedings, (c) privilege at all stages, (d) express exceptions, and (e) partial applicability. Fed. R. Evid. 1101(a)-(e). It contains no provision addressed to proceedings commenced before the effective date. The transition rule for pre-existing cases is statutory — § 1 of Pub. L. No. 93-595 — and it is to that section, not to Rule 1101, that a court must look for the answer to Question 1. A brief that argues the pending-case question from Rule 1101 alone will miss the governing text.

C. Statutory backdrop

The Rules were prescribed by the Supreme Court under the Rules Enabling Act, transmitted to Congress, and — after Congress postponed their operation — enacted with modifications as positive law. Pub. L. No. 93-12, 87 Stat. 9 (Mar. 30, 1973) (postponing effective date) [verify citation]; Pub. L. No. 93-595, 88 Stat. 1926 (Jan. 2, 1975). The Enabling Act as it now reads authorizes rules "of practice and procedure and rules of evidence for cases in the United States district courts (including proceedings before magistrate judges thereof) and courts of appeals." 28 U.S.C. § 2072(a).

=====================================================================
PART IV. QUESTION 1 — DO THE RULES GOVERN FURTHER PROCEDURE IN A PENDING ACTION?
=====================================================================

A. Answer: Yes, presumptively.

Section 1 contains three operative clauses:

(1) Effective date: the Rules take effect on the 180th day after January 2, 1975 — July 1, 1975.
(2) Forward-looking clause: the Rules apply to actions, cases, and proceedings brought after the effective date.
(3) Transition clause: the Rules "also apply to further procedure in actions, cases, and proceedings then pending."

Clause (3) is the answer to Question 1. For a case pending on July 1, 1975, the default rule is application, not preservation of the old law. The party who wants the pre-1975 law must bring himself within the exception in the second half of the sentence.

B. What "further procedure" means

"Further procedure" is procedural-forward language: it reaches steps taken in the case after July 1, 1975 — further pretrial proceedings, trial, and post-trial proceedings — as distinguished from what already happened before that date. Three consequences follow from the text:

1. The Rules do not retroactively govern events completed before July 1, 1975. Evidence already admitted, rulings already made, and records already made up under the former principles are not reopened by clause (3); clause (3) governs what happens next.
2. "Further procedure" is not limited to trial. It is broad enough to include further pretrial and post-trial steps, and, on its face, further proceedings in an appellate court in a case that was pending on July 1, 1975. (The text says "actions, cases, and proceedings then pending," not "trials then pending.")
3. The clause is not time-limited. Nothing in § 1 says the transition rule expires; it operates by reference to the status of the case on July 1, 1975. As a practical matter, however, the further removed the proceeding is from 1975, the weaker any claim that applying the Rules is infeasible or unjust — a point to make to the court.

C. Relationship to Rule 1101

Application of the Rules to a pending action is still subject to Rule 1101's scope limits. If the proceeding is one listed in Rule 1101(d) (for example, a grand-jury proceeding, or a miscellaneous proceeding such as extradition or rendition), the Rules — other than those on privilege — do not apply at all, and § 1's transition clause is never reached. Fed. R. Evid. 1101(c), (d). Conversely, the rules on privilege apply "to all stages of a case or proceeding," Fed. R. Evid. 1101(c), which is the one category where the transition question is most acute (see Part V.F below).

D. Jurisdictional limit

The Rules govern "proceedings in the courts of the United States and before United States bankruptcy judges and United States magistrate judges, to the extent and with the exceptions stated in Rule 1101." Fed. R. Evid. 101; see Fed. R. Evid. 1101(a). Section 1 of Pub. L. No. 93-595 says nothing about state courts. A state evidence code with a similar transition provision requires its own analysis; the federal answer does not carry over.

=====================================================================
PART V. QUESTION 2 — WHAT HAPPENS WHERE APPLICATION WOULD NOT BE FEASIBLE OR WOULD WORK INJUSTICE?
=====================================================================

A. Answer

"Former evidentiary principles apply" — but only "to the extent that" application of the Rules "would not be feasible, or would work injustice." Pub. L. No. 93-595, § 1. The consequence is a substitution of the pre-July 1, 1975 evidentiary law for the Federal Rules, confined to the matters as to which the condition is established. The Rules continue to govern everything else in the further procedure.

B. The trigger is disjunctive and fact-bound

Two independent triggers: (1) application "would not be feasible"; or (2) application "would work injustice." Either suffices; neither is defined in the text. Because the operative judgment is committed to the court applying the Rules, the determination is for the trial court in the first instance, subject on appeal to review for abuse of discretion. Caution: the 1975 text of § 1 does not name the decision-maker, unlike the parallel formula Congress later enacted for Enabling Act rules, which vests the judgment expressly in "the court in which such proceedings are pending." 28 U.S.C. § 2074 (as added by Pub. L. No. 100-702, tit. IV, § 401(a), 102 Stat. 4649, eff. Dec. 1, 1988) [verify section number — see Part VIII]. The later formula is confirmation of Congress's consistent design, not a rule that governs a 1975 action, and should be cited as such.

C. The displacement is partial, not global

The words "to the extent that" are the textual basis for issue-by-issue treatment. A court asked to apply the savings clause should be pressed to identify: (i) the specific rule or rules whose application is said to be infeasible or unjust; (ii) the specific evidentiary question or stage of the proceeding affected; and (iii) the former principle that would govern instead. A blanket request that "the old rules apply to this case" overreads the clause.

D. The standard is not a fairness override

"Would work injustice" is not a license to reach the evidentiary result the court prefers. The clause is a transition mechanism: it addresses dislocation caused by a mid-case change in the governing law. The strongest showing is concrete and procedural — e.g., that a party prepared and conducted an earlier phase of the case in reliance on the former principles in a way that cannot now be undone; that a mid-trial switch would require recalling witnesses or re-opening proofs; that the former principle is embedded in a pretrial order or in the law of the case. The weakest showing is a general assertion that the new Rules are less favorable to one side. The passage of time since 1975 cuts against the clause, not for it.

E. What "former evidentiary principles" means

On its face, the phrase denotes the evidentiary law in force immediately before July 1, 1975: the pre-existing common-law rules of evidence and the pre-existing federal statutory rules on evidence, as they then stood. The text does not say whether statutory provisions that the 1975 Act itself repealed survive as "former evidentiary principles" for pending cases. That question is unresolved on the face of § 1 and is flagged for research (Part VIII).

F. Interaction with the privilege rules

Rule 1101(c) provides that "[t]he rules on privilege apply to all stages of a case or proceeding." Fed. R. Evid. 1101(c). Whether § 1's savings clause can displace a privilege rule in a pending case, given Rule 1101(c)'s "all stages" command, is not answered by either text. Rule 501 supplies the content (common law as interpreted by United States courts, unless the Constitution, a federal statute, or Supreme Court rules provide otherwise; state law governs privilege on state-law claims). Fed. R. Evid. 501. Flagged as an open question; do not assume the savings clause reaches privilege without addressing Rule 1101(c) expressly.

G. Waiver and preservation

The clause is not self-executing in practice. A party who wants the former principles must invoke § 1 and identify the extent of the requested displacement, or risk review only for plain error under Fed. R. Evid. 103(e). The objection must state the specific ground. Fed. R. Evid. 103(a)(1). The practical vehicle is a pretrial motion in limine or a pretrial memorandum designating each evidence question as to which the former principles are said to apply, with the supporting facts. Burden: the text places the condition on the party seeking the exception; assume the movant bears the burden of establishing infeasibility or injustice by a preponderance, and plead accordingly. (This allocation is an inference from the structure of the clause, not a verified holding — see Part VIII.)

=====================================================================
PART VI. MODEL ORDER LANGUAGE (for adaptation)
=====================================================================

"This action was pending on July 1, 1975. Section 1 of the Act of January 2, 1975, Pub. L. No. 93-595, § 1, 88 Stat. 1926, provides that the Federal Rules of Evidence 'also apply to further procedure in actions, cases, and proceedings then pending, except to the extent that application of the rules would not be feasible, or would work injustice, in which event former evidentiary principles apply.' Having considered the parties' submissions, the Court finds:

1. The Federal Rules of Evidence govern further procedure in this action, including the proceedings scheduled for ______.

2. As to the following matters, and to that extent only, application of the Federal Rules of Evidence would [not be feasible] [work injustice] for the reasons stated: ______. As to those matters, the evidentiary principles in force immediately before July 1, 1975 govern, namely: ______.

3. All other evidentiary questions in the further procedure in this action are governed by the Federal Rules of Evidence.

SO ORDERED."

PART VII. CHECKLIST FOR THE MOVING PARTY
=====================================================================

1. Establish the case was pending on July 1, 1975 (docket, file stamp, judgment date).
2. Identify each specific evidence question as to which the former principles are sought, and the rule that would otherwise apply.
3. State the former principle that would govern instead, with a citation to the pre-1975 authority.
4. State the concrete facts showing infeasibility or injustice (reliance, completed phases, embedded pretrial rulings, witness unavailability, prejudice that cannot be cured).
5. Propose a narrow order that displaces the Rules only as to those questions (Part VI).
6. Preserve the objection at the time the evidence is offered, Fed. R. Evid. 103(a)(1), and make an offer of proof where required, Fed. R. Evid. 103(a)(2).

PART VIII. AUTHORITY ASSESSMENT — WHAT IS SOLID AND WHAT IS THIN
=====================================================================

Solid (verified against primary text):
- The full text of § 1 of Pub. L. No. 93-595, including the effective date, the forward-looking clause, and the pending-proceedings clause with its infeasibility/injustice exception and "former evidentiary principles" consequence. 88 Stat. 1926.
- Rule 1101's structure and its silence on pending proceedings. Fed. R. Evid. 1101(a)-(e).
- Rule 101's scope statement. Fed. R. Evid. 101.
- Rule 1101(c) (privilege at all stages). Fed. R. Evid. 1101(c).
- Rule 501 (source of privilege law). Fed. R. Evid. 501.
- 28 U.S.C. § 2072(a) (current Enabling Act authority over rules of evidence).

Thin, conflicting, or unverified — must be cite-checked before any filing:
1. Section number of the 1988 parallel formula. The text ("The Supreme Court may fix the extent such rule shall apply to proceedings then pending, except that the Supreme Court shall not require the application of such rule to further proceedings then pending to the extent that, in the opinion of the court in which such proceedings are pending, the application of such rule in such proceedings would not be feasible or would work injustice, in which event the former rule applies. (b) Any such rule creating, abolishing, or modifying an evidentiary privilege shall have no force or effect unless approved by Act of Congress.") appears immediately before 28 U.S.C. § 2075 in the Code, i.e., at 28 U.S.C. § 2074, added by Pub. L. No. 100-702, tit. IV, § 401(a), 102 Stat. 4649, eff. Dec. 1, 1988. The section heading was not captured in the source I read; confirm the number against the printed Code before citing.
2. Verbatim 1975 text of Rule 1101. The version I read is the amended text; the original enumeration of courts and officers differed (the original referred to the Court of Claims and to United States magistrates and bankruptcy referees). Confirm against 88 Stat. 1926 before quoting Rule 1101 as originally enacted.
3. Case law construing § 1's savings clause. I located no decision construing "further procedure," "not feasible," or "would work injustice" in § 1 of Pub. L. No. 93-595. This is a genuine gap. Run a full-text citator search for "88 Stat. 1926," "Pub. L. 93-595, § 1," and "former evidentiary principles" before asserting that no authority exists.
4. Standard of review and burden allocation (Part V.B, V.G) are inferences from the text and from the parallel 1988 formula, not verified holdings.
5. Survival of repealed pre-1975 evidentiary statutes as "former evidentiary principles" (Part V.E) is unresolved on the face of § 1; check the Act's repealer sections and any interpretive decision.
6. Pub. L. No. 93-12, 87 Stat. 9 (Mar. 30, 1973) (postponement of the proposed Rules) is cited from recollection of the historical sequence and is flagged for verification.

Drafting analogue worth citing by analogy only: when Congress added Rule 502 in 2008, it specified that the amendments apply "in all proceedings commenced after September 19, 2008, and, insofar as is just and practicable, in all proceedings pending on that date." Pub. L. No. 110-322, § 1, 122 Stat. 3537 (Sept. 19, 2008). The "just and practicable" formula is Congress's modern phrasing of the same transition concern and shows that the § 1 formulation is deliberate, not accidental. It does not govern a 1975 action.

=====================================================================
PART IX. WHAT WOULD CHANGE THE ANSWER
=====================================================================

- If the proceeding falls within a Rule 1101(d) exception (grand jury; extradition or rendition; certain other miscellaneous proceedings), the Rules — except those on privilege — do not apply at all, and § 1's transition clause is never reached.
- If the case was commenced after July 1, 1975, the first sentence of § 1 governs and the savings clause is irrelevant.
- If the question concerns a proceeding in state court, § 1 of Pub. L. No. 93-595 does not speak to it; a state analog must be analyzed on its own terms.
- If the question concerns an amendment to the Rules adopted after 1975 (for example, Rule 502), the applicability note to that amendment, not § 1, controls.
